911.title: The fall
911.hook: the Abbasids overthrow the Umayyads violently
911.howItsDone: Muslim historians such as al-Tabari record the fall of the Umayyads in detail, and readers still debate how to judge both dynasties.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Andalus, and armies at both ends of one empire. Your line was 711.

"Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." That's a line from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, from a verse addressed to God as the owner of all power. Some readers hear in it a law of history. The Umayyads had ruled from Damascus through the coins, the offices, the armies at the strait and the Indus. They looked permanent. Then, far to the east, in Khurasan, men began to raise black banners. Today: the fall.
screen: `THOU GIVEST, THOU WITHDRAWEST.` → `THE UMAYYADS LOOKED PERMANENT.` → `BLACK BANNERS IN KHURASAN.`

segments.voice: The movement grew in secret. Its preachers called people to fight for one chosen from the family of Muhammad, and, the histories say, they kept that person's name hidden. Those who answered included people angry at the Umayyads, and some who hoped for a ruler from the line of Ali. A commander called Abu Muslim led the rising in Khurasan, and the black banners moved west. In Kufa, the hidden name was finally spoken. The new caliph was Abu al-Abbas, a descendant of al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle; that's where the name Abbasid comes from. Some who had hoped for a descendant of Ali felt the revolution had been taken from them. Then came the battle by the Zab river, in Iraq. The Umayyad caliph, Marwan, was defeated, fled to Egypt, and was killed there. What followed was not merciful. Al-Tabari reports that members of the Umayyad family were hunted down, and that at one gathering where they had been promised safety, they were killed. The histories set this down plainly, and Muslim writers since have not always agreed on how to judge it. So the day carries two things. A dynasty that had come to power at the end of one civil war lost it in another. The verse speaks of power given and withdrawn; the histories record how this power changed hands. Both sit in this story at once. Dynasties fall.
screen: `A HIDDEN NAME FROM THE PROPHET'S FAMILY.` · `THE NAME IS SPOKEN IN KUFA.` · `THE BATTLE BY THE ZAB.` · then, large: `DYNASTIES FALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something in your life that feels permanent, a job, a role, a way things have always been at home, and notice, gently, that it had a beginning and will have an end too, without arguing with the thought or sinking into it. Then ask: if this ended, what would I want to have done well while I held it? If you pray, bring that question to God in your own words.
The fall. The violent end of Umayyad rule, when the Abbasids, raising black banners in the name of the Prophet's family, took the caliphate. Today's word.
Your line: dynasties fall. Even the ones that look permanent. Day nine hundred eleven, done.

912.title: The one who escaped
912.hook: Abd al-Rahman, an Umayyad prince, escapes to Spain and founds a new state
912.howItsDone: The story of Abd al-Rahman's escape and his palm-tree poem is retold in histories of al-Andalus, and the Great Mosque of Cordoba, which tradition says he began, still stands.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fall, black banners and the end of Umayyad rule. Your line was dynasties fall.

A young man is sitting in a house near the Euphrates when his small son runs in, frightened. Outside, black banners: the Abbasid horsemen have come for what is left of the Umayyad family. He grabs his younger brother and they run for the river. They plunge in and swim. From the bank, the soldiers shout: come back, you're safe, nobody will harm you. The younger brother, tired and afraid of drowning, turns back. The older one keeps swimming. From the far bank, the histories say, he watched them kill his brother. His name was Abd al-Rahman, a grandson of the caliph Hisham. Today: the one who escaped.
screen: `BLACK BANNERS OUTSIDE.` → `INTO THE EUPHRATES.` → `ONE TURNS BACK, ONE SWIMS ON.`

segments.voice: What do you do when everything you belonged to is gone? Abd al-Rahman went west. The Andalusian histories say he traveled in hiding through North Africa with a freedman named Badr, staying for a time with his mother's people, the Berbers, and slipping away when local rulers grew suspicious. Al-Andalus, across the strait, was full of quarreling factions, and among them were old clients and supporters of the Umayyad house. Badr crossed first to sound them out. Then Abd al-Rahman landed. He gathered supporters, defeated the governor, and entered Cordoba as its ruler. He didn't claim to be caliph. He ruled as emir, and the state he founded would last long after him. People gave him a nickname, al-Dakhil, the one who entered. And there's a tender story people tell. In a garden near Cordoba, he is said to have planted a palm tree, the kind that grew back in Syria, and written lines of poetry to it. In the poem, as the story goes, he speaks to the palm as a fellow stranger: you too are far from your home, brought to a land not your own. So the founder of a state is remembered talking to a tree about homesickness. He lost much of his family, his city and his world, and he did not get them back. He started again, in a new place, with what he carried.
screen: `WEST THROUGH NORTH AFRICA.` · `BADR CROSSES FIRST.` · `CORDOBA, AND AN EMIR.` · then, large: `A PALM FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time something ended for you, a move, a loss, a door that closed, and notice what you carried out of it, even something small: a habit, a friend, a skill, a stubbornness. If you pray, ask for strength for new beginnings in your own words; if you don't, just let what you carried be counted.

913.title: The round city
913.hook: the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad as a round city on the Tigris
913.howItsDone: Historians reconstruct the round city of Baghdad from written descriptions by al-Tabari, al-Ya'qubi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, since little or nothing of it can be seen today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Dakhil, who swam the Euphrates and began again in al-Andalus. Your line was he started again.

Night, on the bank of the Tigris. Workers have marked out the plan of a city on the bare ground with lines of ash. Now, al-Tabari reports, the caliph orders the lines laid over with cotton seeds soaked in naphtha, and set alight. The whole plan of the city flares up in fire on the dark earth, so the caliph can walk it and see it whole before a single brick is laid. And the shape burning in the dark is a circle. The caliph is al-Mansur, of the new Abbasid house, and the city is Baghdad. Today: the round city.
screen: `LINES OF ASH ON THE GROUND.` → `SET ALIGHT AT NIGHT.` → `A CIRCLE OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: Why a new city? The Abbasids had overthrown a dynasty based in Damascus, and their strength lay east, in Iraq and Khurasan. Al-Mansur wanted a capital of his own. He chose a spot on the Tigris, where boats and roads could bring the trade of many lands, and gave it an official name: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Some readers hear in it an echo of the Qur'an, where God is said to call people to the abode of peace. Then the shape. The old descriptions tell of a city ringed by walls, with gates opening onto the great roads, each named for where its road led: the Kufa gate, the Basra gate, the Khurasan gate, the Syria gate. At the very center stood the caliph's palace, crowned by a green dome, with the great mosque beside it. The ruler sits at the center, and the great roads of the empire run to his door: a city drawn as a picture of power. Yet the circle didn't hold. Markets and neighborhoods spilled out past the walls almost from the start, and Baghdad grew in every direction, across the river and beyond. The round city itself is long gone, known now only from the descriptions of writers who saw it or heard about it. A perfect circle, drawn in fire, and then the life of a real city overflowing it.
screen: `A CAPITAL OF THEIR OWN.` · `THE CITY OF PEACE.` · `GATES TO THE FOUR ROADS.` · then, large: `THE PALACE AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: If you have paper and a pen, draw a circle as round as you can, knowing it won't be perfect, and put a dot at the center. Ask what sits at the center of your days right now, work, worry, a person, a phone, and what you'd want there instead. If you pray, bring to mind the name the city was given, the City of Peace, and ask for peace in your own words.

914.title: Harun al-Rashid
914.hook: the caliph of the Thousand and One Nights legends, and of real scholars and envoys
914.howItsDone: Readers around the world still enjoy the Thousand and One Nights as story, while historians read al-Tabari, Abu Yusuf's book on taxation and the Frankish annals to reconstruct the real Harun.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Mansur's round Baghdad, its plan traced on the ground in lines of fire. Your line was a circle, drawn in fire.

A caliph slips out of his palace at night, dressed as a merchant. With him are his vizier, Ja'far, and his swordbearer, Masrur. They wander the lanes of Baghdad, overhear a fisherman's troubles, knock on a strange door, and stumble into an adventure that ends with the caliph revealing who he is and setting everything right. That's Harun al-Rashid as readers have long met him, in the stories of the Thousand and One Nights. But there was a real Harun, who ruled from Baghdad and left traces in histories, law books, and even the records of a king in Europe. Today: telling the two apart.
screen: `A CALIPH IN DISGUISE.` → `JA'FAR AND MASRUR.` → `THE STORIES, AND THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Start with what the histories say. Al-Tabari records that Harun led pilgrimages to Mecca and also led campaigns against the Byzantine empire on his frontier. His wife Zubayda is remembered for paying for wells and water stations along the pilgrim road from Iraq. Then the scholars. The jurist Abu Yusuf, a student of Abu Hanifa, wrote a book on taxation and public finance addressed to Harun, advising him how to collect revenue fairly. Then the envoys. Annals kept at the court of Charlemagne, the Frankish ruler, record that Harun's embassy brought Charlemagne gifts, among them an elephant named Abul Abaz. Now the hardest real story. Ja'far, the friendly vizier of the tales, was a real man, from the powerful Barmakid family who helped run the empire. The histories report that Harun suddenly had Ja'far executed and brought the whole family down. They give different reasons, and the cause is still uncertain. So the real Harun was pious and warlike, generous and frightening, a patron of scholars and a ruler who could destroy his closest friend overnight. The tales soften him into the wise night-walker who fixes everything. The stories are wonderful stories. But they are not evidence. Holding them apart is a skill: enjoy the legend as legend, and read history as history, with its gaps and its blood left in. Legend and history.
screen: `PILGRIM AND SOLDIER.` · `A LAW BOOK ADDRESSED TO HIM.` · `AN ELEPHANT FOR CHARLEMAGNE.` · then, large: `THE FALL OF THE BARMAKIDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a story told about someone famous, or about your own family, the grandparent who did something remarkable, the founder who started with nothing, and ask: what do I actually know happened, and what has been polished in the telling? You don't need to throw the story away; just hold the two piles side by side. If you pray, you can ask for honesty in how you tell your own stories.

915.title: The House of Wisdom
915.hook: a Baghdad center where scholars translated and studied Greek, Persian and Indian works
915.howItsDone: Muslim scholars point to the House of Wisdom and the translation movement when they talk about learning from other peoples, and historians study the surviving Arabic translations and Hunayn's own letter about his work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Harun al-Rashid, the caliph of the tales and the ruler of the histories. Your line was legend and history.

A caliph dreams that a man is sitting on his bed: fair-skinned and broad-browed. The caliph asks who he is. Aristotle, the man says. The caliph asks him, what is good? The dream-Aristotle answers in steps: first, whatever reason finds good; then, whatever the religious law finds good; then, whatever people find good. The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim tells this story about the caliph al-Ma'mun, Harun's son, as one reason Greek books were sought out and brought to Baghdad. Whether or not the dream happened, the books really came, and something in Baghdad took them in. It had a name: Bayt al-Hikmah. Today: the House of Wisdom.
screen: `A CALIPH'S DREAM.` → `WHAT IS GOOD?` → `BOOKS BROUGHT TO BAGHDAD.`

segments.voice: Bayt al-Hikmah means the House of Wisdom. Start with a caution: historians argue about what it actually was. A palace library? A translation office? A meeting place for scholars? The sources are thin, and it may have been smaller than its fame. What isn't in doubt is the work done in Baghdad in those generations. Books in Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit were turned into Arabic: Euclid's geometry, Ptolemy's astronomy, the medicine of Galen, the philosophy of Aristotle, Persian wisdom literature, Indian astronomy and numbers. The people doing the work were not all Muslims. One well-known translator, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, was a Christian physician. In a letter about his work, he describes hunting for several copies of a book by Galen and comparing them before he translated, because copies differ and mistakes creep in. A later writer, al-Safadi, describes his way as carrying over the meaning of a whole sentence, not swapping word for word. Muslim scholars took up these books, argued with them, corrected them and built on them, in mathematics, medicine and philosophy. Why would a Muslim court spend so much on foreign books? Some readers point to the Qur'an, which says God gives wisdom to whom He wills, and that whoever is given wisdom has been given much good. Wisdom, on that view, isn't owned by one people. It's a gift you go looking for. Wisdom from everywhere.
screen: `WHAT WAS IT, REALLY?` · `GREEK, PERSIAN, INDIAN, INTO ARABIC.` · `HUNAYN COMPARES THE COPIES.` · then, large: `WISDOM IS A GIFT TO SEEK.`

916.title: Paper from Samarkand
916.hook: papermaking spreads west, and books become cheaper
916.howItsDone: Historians of the book study surviving paper manuscripts from the Muslim world, and calligraphers today still prepare paper by hand for copying the Qur'an and other texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bayt al-Hikmah, and Hunayn comparing his copies of Galen. Your line was wisdom from everywhere.

A receipt. A sticky note. A shopping list on the back of an envelope. Paper is so ordinary now that it gets thrown away by the handful. Yet for a long time, writing something down meant writing on something costly: the scraped and dried skin of an animal, or papyrus reeds that grew along the Nile. Every page had a price. All those translations in Baghdad needed something to be written on. The answer came from the east, by way of a city on the Silk Road called Samarkand. Today: warraqun, the paper people.
screen: `A RECEIPT, A STICKY NOTE.` → `ONCE, EVERY PAGE HAD A PRICE.` → `SOMETHING CAME FROM THE EAST.`

segments.voice: Paper came from China, made from plant fibers and rags beaten into pulp, spread thin on a screen, and dried. Later writers tell a story about how it reached the Muslim world: after a battle in Central Asia, Chinese prisoners were brought to Samarkand, and some of them knew how to make paper and taught the craft there. It's a good story. Historians question it, and some think the knowledge traveled more slowly, along trade routes. Either way, Samarkand paper became known, and before long paper was being made in Baghdad too. The historian Ibn Khaldun says that the Barmakid minister al-Fadl ibn Yahya, from the family in Harun's story, had government records written on paper. Now see what that did. Paper was cheaper than skin and easier to come by than papyrus. Cheaper paper meant cheaper books. Baghdad grew a market of booksellers and copyists, called warraqun, the paper people. The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim, whose catalog told of al-Ma'mun's dream, was one of them. Scholars could own more books, students could copy their teachers' lectures, and the translations of the House of Wisdom could travel. The Qur'an speaks of God, in Pickthall's words, "Who teacheth by the pen." A pen needs a page. In this story, the page got cheap, and learning spread. Paper changed everything.

917.title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
917.hook: the mathematician whose name gives us algorithm and whose book gives us algebra
917.howItsDone: Muslim scholars working in Baghdad wrote practical mathematics for daily needs, and inheritance law, with its shares named in the Qur'an, was one of the problems their arithmetic served.

segments.voice: Yesterday, warraqun, the paper people, and paper from Samarkand: a cheaper page, and suddenly more people could own a book. Your line was: paper changed everything.

A man has died and left his estate: some land, some coins, a debt to settle, a bequest to a friend. His widow, his daughters and his mother are waiting. The Qur'an names their shares in fractions, and somebody has to turn those fractions into actual coins in actual hands, with nobody cheated. Now multiply that by every family in a city. In Baghdad, a scholar at the caliph's court wrote a short book for exactly this kind of problem. His name was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, and a strange word in his book's title ended up in schoolbooks everywhere.
screen: `AN ESTATE TO DIVIDE.` → `SHARES IN FRACTIONS.` → `A BOOK TO HELP.`

segments.voice: The book is usually called the short book on calculating by al-jabr and al-muqabala. In his opening, al-Khwarizmi says why he wrote it: for what people need every day, in inheritance and wills, dividing property, lawsuits and trade, measuring land and digging canals. A practical book, full of worked examples. Al-jabr and al-muqabala are two moves. Al-jabr means restoring, setting right what is broken: when one side of a problem has something taken away, you add the missing piece back to both sides, so the problem is whole again. Al-muqabala means balancing: when the same kind of thing sits on both sides, you take it off both, and what remains is simpler and still fair. Restore, then balance, and the unknown comes into the open. The usual account is that Latin readers later kept al-jabr from the title, and it became our word algebra. And dictionaries trace the author's own name, the man from Khwarazm, to our word algorithm, a step-by-step method. The two moves share something with a court of law, or a family dividing an inheritance: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. The Qur'an asks people to keep the measure and not cut short the balance. This week we watched a dynasty fall, a young man escape and start again, a round city rise, and the House of Wisdom gather books on cheap new paper. Here is what grew there: a way of thinking that restores and balances.
screen: `A BOOK FOR EVERYDAY NEEDS.` · `AL-JABR: RESTORING.` · `AL-MUQABALA: BALANCING.` · `WHAT YOU DO TO ONE SIDE, DO TO THE OTHER.` · then, large: `RESTORING AND BALANCING.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper, and write a simple sum with a missing number: something plus three makes ten. Now do the balancing move: take three from both sides, keep the scale level, and write what's left. Sit with the page and notice its steadiness, one side and the other kept equal; if you pray, you can begin with bismillah, and if not, just breathe with the balance.
Al-Khwarizmi. The scholar in Baghdad's House of Wisdom whose book of al-jabr, restoring, and al-muqabala, balancing, gave us the word algebra. Today's word.
Your line: restoring and balancing. Fair to both sides, and the unknown comes clear. Day nine hundred seventeen, done.
